summary: This RFC proposes the Reliable Asynchronous Transfer Protocol, which lets two programs communicate reliably over a link so data arrives intact and unaltered. It targets asynchronous serial links. It asked for comments and is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 916 defines RATP, a way for two programs to send each other data reliably over a serial line such as a modem connection. The protocol checks every packet with a checksum and resends anything that goes wrong or goes missing, and it can tell the other end how much data it is willing to accept at once. The design deliberately keeps things simple so that small machines and simple devices can run it.

questions: what is the reliable asynchronous transfer protocol
how does ratp handle noisy serial links
subtitle: A small stop-and-wait protocol that makes a noisy telephone line carry data reliably.

tldr.problem: Personal computers of the early 1980s had RS-232 ports and modems but usually no network connection, and the telephone network they would use was built for voice. Noise on such a line corrupts bytes and inserts spurious ones, so data sent over it needs checking and resending.
tldr.mechanism: RATP sends one packet at a time in each direction over a full duplex point-to-point link. Each packet starts with a synchronisation octet, carries control flags and a one-bit sequence number, and ends with a 16-bit checksum of the data. A packet is resent if its acknowledgement does not arrive before a timer expires.
tldr.outcome: RFC 916 is Historic and the RFC Editor recommends it for no further use. It was a proposed protocol rather than a standard, and its editor's note says it was set aside in 1983 and distributed again because of the Thinwire proposal described in RFC 914.

today: RFC 916 is Historic, which means the RFC Editor recommends it for no further use. It was a proposed protocol rather than a standard, and its editor's note says it was prepared in essentially this form in June 1983, set aside, and distributed again because of the Thinwire proposal described in RFC 914.

sections.title: Why Another Protocol for a Noisy Line
sections.content:
The memo starts from the situation it was written for. Cheap personal computers were usually stand-alone, but virtually all of them had an RS-232 interface and a modem, which let them talk to each other over the telephone. The telephone system is a pervasive network, but the standard circuit was designed for voice and tolerates far more noise than a data circuit does. It is therefore not uncommon for a byte transferred over a telephone circuit to have noise inserted, or for spurious data bytes to be added to the stream.

The design decisions were made by ensuring reliability first and then favouring simplicity of implementation, so that the protocol could be implemented by small computers and by stand-alone devices that accept commands over RS-232 lines. Sophisticated but unnecessary features such as dynamic window management were left out, several packets outstanding at a time were eliminated for the same reason, and data queued to send when a connection is closed remotely is discarded. Those choices remove two states from the implementation.

The memo then explains why a new protocol was defined at all, since RS-232 transport protocols were already in use. Some of them can only transfer data in one direction, which means a single RS-232 link cannot be used for a full duplex connection, cannot act as a bridge between most computer networks, and cannot support applications needing two-way exchange; unidirectional flow is enough for a weak file transfer but not for remote terminal service or transaction processing. Some allow only fixed size packets, or do not let the receiver limit the sender's packet size, and where that block size is too large for the receiving concentrator the concentrator is likely to invoke flow control immediately, resulting in many dropped and damaged packets. Some have features that may or may not be implemented at each site, such as several checksumming algorithms or differing data transmission restrictions, and the requirement that every site implement every feature is rarely met.

The protocol is designed to operate on any point-to-point link capable of transmitting and receiving data, and it is not necessary that the link be asynchronous, but because neither end controls when the other transmits it should be full duplex. In practice an asynchronous full duplex RS-232 link was expected. Because the protocol operates in a point-to-point environment it comprises both the datagram and reliable connection layers, and no multi-network capability is implied; where a link using this protocol bridges differing networks, other protocols such as TCP are expected to have their packets fragmented and encapsulated inside the packets of this protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol exists because telephone lines are noisy and because the serial protocols of the day each fell short in a different way: some only carried data one way, some used fixed packet sizes the receiver could not refuse, and some offered options that different sites did not all implement. RATP is deliberately plain. It sends one packet at a time, resends what goes missing, and leaves out anything clever.

sections.title: The Packet: Header, Data and Checksums
sections.content:
RATP transmits data over a full duplex link, in both directions. A stream of data is communicated by being broken into 8-bit pieces called octets, which are accumulated serially to form a packet, and the packet is the unit of data communicated over the link. The protocol virtually guarantees that data transmitted at one end, if received, arrives unaltered and intact at the other end. All eight bits of an octet contain data and must be preserved by the link interface and device driver, which in many operating systems is arranged by putting the connection into RAW or BINARY data mode. During normal operation packets are transmitted and acknowledged one at a time over the link in each direction, and each packet is a header followed by a data portion that may be empty.

The header is four octets. The first is the Synch Leader, the one octet hex 01, the ASCII Start Of Header character. Because RS-232 is a self-clocking medium and the wires are often in noisy environments where noise appears as added unwanted data, the start of a packet is marked with this pattern so the receiver can discard what came before it. The pattern is a compromise, since different modems respond to noise differently, and a spurious SYNCH can be seen, which is why a header checksum is provided. The second octet holds the control flags and the sequence numbers, the third holds the data length, and the fourth holds the header checksum.

The control octet contains the SYN flag to synchronise the connection, the ACK flag whose acknowledge number is significant, the RST flag to reset the connection, the FIN flag meaning that no more data will be sent or accepted, the one-bit sequence number SN and the one-bit acknowledge number AN, the EOR flag which is an aid for higher level protocols that fragment their packets, and the SO flag for a packet carrying a single octet of data. The text describes the octet as a 5-bit field of control flags and two 1-bit sequence number fields, with the last bit reserved and required to be zero. No data may be sent in a packet with the SYN, RST or FIN flag set, and the EOR bit is for information only, to be set or cleared by the higher layer.

The SO flag exists for single character transmission, where rapid interactive response means many keystrokes are sent one at a time. If SO is set the packet holds exactly one octet of data, so the LENGTH field is superfluous and carries the data octet itself, and the data portion is not transmitted. Without the SO flag seven octets would be required; with it only four are needed, so transmission efficiency is improved by 40 percent, and the header checksum protects the single octet.

The length octet holds the MDL, the maximum number of data octets the receiver is allowed to transmit in any single packet, when the SYN bit is present, so a sender can indicate its unwillingness to accept any data by specifying an MDL of zero. Otherwise, if neither SYN, RST nor FIN is set, it is an 8-bit LENGTH field holding the count of data octets in the packet, from zero to the MDL, and the MDL is limited to a maximum of 255. The header checksum is the 8-bit equivalent of the 16-bit data checksum, built the same way, over the control, length and header checksum octets, not including the SYNCH pattern; the receiver accepts the header only if the sum is octal 377.

The data portion follows the header when the SO flag is not set and LENGTH is greater than zero. It consists of LENGTH data octets immediately followed by two data checksum octets, so that the data portion contains LENGTH+2 octets. The 16-bit data checksum detects incorrectly transmitted data, and the probability of an error of the bit drop out or bit insertion kind going undetected is on the order of 2**(-16). The checksum octets follow the data so that the sender can compute the checksum while transmitting and the receiver while receiving, so that neither has to store the packet and process it again. The octets are assembled into 16-bit words in big endian order. The algorithm is the one used by IP and TCP: the unsigned sum of the 16-bit words of the data portion is formed, any overflow is added into the lowest order bit, and the result is complemented and inserted into the checksum field; the receiver performs the same sum including the received checksum field and accepts the data only if the sum is octal 177777. An odd number of data octets is padded on the right with zeros for checksum purposes, and the pad octet is not transmitted.

Sequence numbers work with acknowledge numbers to tell the sender that its last data packet was received and to tell the receiver the sequence number of the next data packet it expects. When the ACK flag is set, the AN field holds the next sequence number the sender of the packet expects to receive, so the sender can tell whether its packet was acknowledged. The receiver expects the next data packet to carry the sequence number given in the AN field of the last acknowledgement it sent; if not, it assumes it is receiving a duplicate of a packet it already acknowledged, and discards it. Only packets containing status flags or data require acknowledgement. Both the AN and SN fields are a single bit wide, because at most one packet is being sent or acknowledged in a particular direction at any one time, and the arithmetic is modulo 2. The maximum packet size is SYNCH plus HEADER plus Data Checksum plus 255, which is 261 octets, so there is no need to allocate more storage for any received packet.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet has four bytes of header and then the data. The first byte marks the start of the packet so that noise before it can be thrown away. The second byte holds the flags, such as synchronise, reset and finish, along with a one-bit sequence number. The third byte says how much data follows, and the fourth checks the header. The data itself ends with a two-byte checksum computed as the sender transmits and checked as the receiver receives, so the packet never has to be stored and read twice.

sections.title: Opening and Closing a Connection
sections.content:
A three-way handshake establishes the connection. It is normally initiated by one end and responded to by the other, and it still works if both sides initiate it at once. Experience has shown that this strategy reduces the probability of false connections to an acceptably low level.

The simplest form runs as follows. Side A, in the CLOSED state, has an open request from its user and sends a SYN packet to side B, which is in the LISTEN state, specifying its initial sequence number, here zero, and placing in the LENGTH field the MDL, the largest number of data octets it can consume in any one packet. Sending it puts A in the SYN-SENT state. When B receives the SYN it enters SYN-RECEIVED and sends a SYN packet that acknowledges the SYN it just received, with the AN field showing it now expects SN=1, and states its own MDL in the LENGTH field. When A receives that packet it enters ESTABLISHED, and can be confident that B expects to receive more packets. A is then free to send the first data packet, and when B receives it, B enters ESTABLISHED. Data cannot be sent before that, because the LENGTH field is being used to specify the MDL while the connection is being opened.

If both ends perform an active open at once, neither is in LISTEN and both send SYN packets. During a simultaneous connection both sides cycle from CLOSED through SYN-SENT and SYN-RECEIVED to ESTABLISHED, and the connection is successfully initiated.

A half-open connection is detected when one computer crashes after a connection is established and then, after recovering, attempts to open a new connection. The other end must recognise the condition and treat it as an error: the new SYN is answered with a RST and ACK, the connection is aborted, and the recovering end sees the connection refused.

Either side may close an established connection by sending a packet with the FIN control bit set. No data may appear in a FIN packet. The other end shuts down its end and replies with a FIN and ACK. The side that closed enters FIN-WAIT, the other enters LAST-ACK, and on receiving the FIN and ACK the closing side answers with an ACK and enters TIME-WAIT, while the other side reaches CLOSED. After waiting to be sure its last acknowledgement was received, the closing side goes to CLOSED as well, after 2*SRTT time has passed, where SRTT is the Smoothed Round Trip Time. If data remains unsent when the user issues the close, the message "Warning: Unsent data remains." is communicated to the user.
sections.plainLanguage: Opening a connection takes three messages: one to start, one that starts and acknowledges at the same time, and one that acknowledges that. Each side says in the same message how much data it is willing to receive. If both sides start at once the exchange still works out, and if one machine has crashed and comes back the other recognises the mismatch and refuses the connection. Closing is the same idea in reverse, with a finish flag that carries no data and a waiting period at the end so that a lost acknowledgement does not reopen a closed connection.

sections.title: Receiving a Packet
sections.content:
Receiving a packet proceeds in three stages. First, synch detection: octets are read continuously and discarded until the SYNCH pattern is seen, and then the header reception stage begins. Second, header reception: the remainder of the header is three octets long and no further processing can continue until the complete header has been read. The header checksum test is then performed. If it fails, the current SYNCH pattern is assumed to be the result of a data error, and since the correct SYNCH may appear immediately after the current one, the receiver goes back to synch detection but treats the three header octets following the bad SYNCH as new input. If the checksum test succeeds, the data reception stage begins.

Third, data reception: the remaining length of the packet is worked out. If any of the SYN, RST, SO or FIN flags are set, the entire packet has already been read and is considered to have arrived, because no data portion of a packet is present when one of those flags is set. Otherwise the LENGTH field specifies how much data to read, and if it is zero the packet has arrived. With a data portion present, the LENGTH+2 octets including the data checksum are read, and the data checksum test is performed. If the test fails the entire packet is discarded and the receiver returns to synch detection; if it succeeds the packet has arrived. Once arrived, the packet is released to the upper level protocol software, and in a multiprocess implementation packet reception begins again at the synch detection stage.
sections.plainLanguage: Incoming bytes are thrown away until the start-of-header byte appears. The next three bytes are the rest of the header and are checked against a checksum; if they do not add up, they were probably noise, so the receiver carries on scanning and treats them as new input. The header says how much data to expect, and that amount is read and checked against the data checksum. A packet that fails either check is discarded and the scan starts again.

sections.title: States, Transitions and Timers
sections.content:
A connection can be modelled as a state machine: each state represents a known point in the history of a connection, and the connection passes from state to state in response to events, which are user calls to the protocol interface, incoming packets and timeouts. The information needed for the successful operation of a connection is called the Transmission Control Block, or TCB, following the terminology of TCP. The user requests to the protocol interface are OPEN, SEND, RECEIVE, ABORT, STATUS and CLOSE.

The states are LISTEN, waiting for a connection from the other end; SYN-SENT, waiting for a matching connection request after having sent one; SYN-RECEIVED, waiting for a confirming acknowledgement after having both received and sent a connection request; ESTABLISHED, the normal state for data transfer; FIN-WAIT, waiting for a termination request from the other end and for an acknowledgement of one already sent; LAST-ACK, having seen and acknowledged a termination request and sent one of its own; CLOSING, waiting for an acknowledgement of a termination request; TIME-WAIT, waiting long enough to be sure the other end received the acknowledgement of its termination request; and CLOSED, a fictional state representing a completely terminated connection, in which neither end sends or receives data or control packets.

Three timers are associated with the protocol. The user timeout is desirable for practical reasons: without an overriding timeout, a connection so noisy that no data gets through, or one physically cut, would result in unbounded retransmissions. When it expires the user is informed "Error: Connection aborted due to user timeout.", all queues are flushed, the TCB is deleted and the CLOSED state is entered.

The retransmission timeout ensures that any packet sent for which the SN is significant is acknowledged. When such a packet is sent it is placed in a retransmission queue and the timer is begun; if no acknowledgement has arrived within the period, the packet is retransmitted and the timer restarted, and if the acknowledgement does arrive in time the timer is stopped and the packet is removed from the queue, so that the next packet with a significant SN may be sent. This timeout is expected to operate with a counter of how many times a packet has been retransmitted. Normally an upper limit is set, and if it is exceeded the connection is aborted with the message "Error: Connection aborted due to retransmission failure", the queues flushed, the TCB deleted and the CLOSED state entered.

The TIME-WAIT timeout catches any FIN packets retransmitted from the other end in response to a dropped acknowledgement packet. The period should be at least as long as 2*SRTT; after it expires the other end is assumed to be closed, the TCB is deleted and this end enters the CLOSED state as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends keep a record of the connection called a transmission control block, and the protocol is described as a set of states that the record moves between as packets arrive, the user asks for things, or timers expire. Three timers matter: one the user sets, which gives up on a connection that has gone quiet; one that resends a packet whose acknowledgement never came, up to a limit; and one that waits after closing so that a repeated finish message is not mistaken for a new connection.

sections.title: Data Error Handling
sections.content:
The data errors an established connection may encounter are distinct from protocol errors, and are listed as framing errors, a missing SYNCH pattern, unacknowledged packets, bad packets, duplicate packets, traffic outside flow control, packets that are too large and packets that are too small.

RS-232 provides framing only for an individual octet, and no pattern was chosen to mark the end of a packet, because any bit pattern can appear in the data and a terminating pattern could not be allowed to appear in the data. The end of the packet is therefore determined synthetically: the start is marked by the SYNCH pattern and the expected end can only be determined by examining the LENGTH octet of the header. Whether LENGTH can be trusted is established by the one octet header checksum covering the first two octets after the SYNCH pattern. If the header passes the checksum test and none of the SYN, FIN, RST nor SO flags are set, then LENGTH is trusted and the number of octets expected beyond the header is LENGTH+2. If the header fails the checksum test the length may be too small or too large, and the receiver rescan for the next SYNCH pattern immediately after the bad one, throwing away octets until a SYNCH is seen and then attempting to reinterpret it as a packet; the sender's retransmission timeout guarantees that a new copy of the packet will be transmitted, so the SYNCH pattern from the retransmitted packet will eventually be seen. This strategy costs nothing unless data errors occur, and removes the overhead of both sender and receiver passing over the data looking for a termination pattern.

If an ACK for a packet is not obtained within the retransmission timeout interval, that packet is retransmitted. Because significant variability in response can be expected from either end, it is best to calculate the interval dynamically. A realistic upper bound time depends on the packet size and the line speed: if the baud rate is 300 or above, with B the baud rate, L the MDL of the receiver and P the packet processing time of the receiver, an Upper Bound for the Reception Time is UBRT = L/(B/10) seconds + P seconds, and a realistic upper bound time is 2*UBRT seconds. For the retransmission timeout itself, the protocol needs a clock with at least single second resolution. The Round Trip Time is measured between sending a packet with a particular SN and receiving an ACK whose AN covers that SN. A Smoothed Round Trip Time is calculated as SRTT = (ALPHA * SRTT) + ((1- ALPHA) * RTT), and the Retransmission Time Out as RTO = min[UBOUND, max[LBOUND, (BETA * SRTT)]], where UBOUND is an upper bound on the timeout, for example 1 minute, LBOUND a lower bound, for example 1 second, ALPHA a smoothing factor, for example .8 to .9, and BETA a delay variance factor, for example 1.3 to 2.0.

A bad packet is one that fails either the header or the data checksum test, and the sender will retransmit it after the retransmission timeout interval. A duplicate packet is one that passes the checksum tests but whose SN is significant and not the expected value, which normally happens when the sender did not get the last ACK from the receiver. The receiver detects the duplicate, discards it and immediately retransmits its own last packet, which the sender then receives.
sections.plainLanguage: Because there is no end marker in the data, the receiver works out where a packet ends from the length field in the header, and it trusts that length only if the header checksum passed. If the header is damaged the receiver scans ahead for the next start-of-header byte, and the sender's resend eventually provides a good copy. The time to wait before resending is worked out from how long packets are actually taking to come back, smoothed over several exchanges so that one slow reply does not set the timeout too low.

fields.name: Synch Leader
fields.desc: One octet, hex 01, the ASCII Start Of Header character. Marks the start of a packet.

fields.name: Control
fields.desc: SYN, ACK, FIN, RST, SN, AN, EOR and SO. The sequence numbers are one bit each.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: The number of data octets, or the MDL the receiver will accept when SYN is set.

fields.name: Header Checksum
fields.desc: An 8-bit end-around carry sum over the control, length and checksum octets.

messages.label: SYN
messages.note: Side A opens the connection and states the largest packet it can accept.

messages.label: SYN, ACK
messages.note: Side B acknowledges that SYN and states its own limit.

messages.label: ACK WITH DATA
messages.note: Side A is established and may send data.
